hed: East-West still offline as Monday crude surges; Yanbu stocks measured in days
dek: Saudi Arabia’s East-West (Petroline) pipeline remained shut Monday after Thursday’s Iraq-origin drone hits near Riyadh and Medina, removing the kingdom’s main Hormuz-bypass export route as Brent jumped toward $108. Traders and Saudi oil buyers told Reuters that Yanbu Red Sea stocks may sustain exports only about five to seven days without a restart, putting up to roughly 4% of global supply at risk. Repair timelines still diverge in reporting — days to weeks — and Saudi officials have not announced a reopen date. NBC News said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday.

cl.body: Reuters, NBC News, and Channel News Asia keep the Monday focus on supply math: Petroline still offline, Yanbu stocks measured in days, and up to ~4% of global oil at risk while Hormuz traffic stays thin — with Monday’s Brent surge as markets price the dual-chokepoint squeeze rather than a confirmed reopen timeline from Riyadh.

cr.body: The National’s Monday oil wrap, Anadolu’s Iraq launch-platform reporting, and NBC’s Jeddah note on MBS meeting Adm. Cooper frame the outage as a live export-security crisis: the Hormuz bypass is dark, crude is printing near $108, and Gulf diplomacy over shipping lanes was postponed the same morning.

stack_blurb: East-West still shut Monday; Yanbu stocks days left; Brent toward $108.
seo_description: Saudi East-West pipeline remains offline Monday as Brent nears $108; Reuters sources say Yanbu stocks may last only days, risking up to ~4% of global supply.
